content: 1. Fatalities associated with the use of albendazole have been reported, primarily due to conditions such as granulocytopenia or pancytopenia. 2. Albendazole has been shown to cause bone marrow suppression, aplastic anemia, and agranulocytosis in patients, regardless of whether they have underlying hepatic dysfunction. 3. Blood counts should be monitored at the start of each 28-day treatment cycle and every two weeks during therapy in all patients. 4. Patients with liver disease, including hepatic echinococcosis, are at a higher risk of bone marrow suppression, which can lead to pancytopenia, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, and leukopenia. These patients require closer monitoring of blood counts. 5. Albendazole therapy should be discontinued in all patients if clinically significant decreases in blood cell counts occur. 6. Albendazole should not be used in pregnant women unless no alternative treatment options are available. 7. Women should avoid becoming pregnant for at least one month after stopping albendazole therapy. 8. If a patient becomes pregnant while taking albendazole, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and the patient should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. 9. Patients being treated for neurocysticercosis should receive appropriate steroid and anticonvulsant therapy as needed. 10. Oral or intravenous corticosteroids should be considered to prevent cerebral hypertensive episodes during the first week of anticysticercal therapy. 11. Pre-existing neurocysticercosis may be uncovered in patients treated with albendazole for other conditions, potentially leading to symptoms such as seizures, increased intracranial pressure, or focal neurological signs due to an inflammatory reaction caused by the death of the parasite in the brain. 12. Symptoms of neurocysticercosis may occur shortly after treatment begins, and appropriate steroid and anticonvulsant therapy should be initiated immediately. 13. In rare cases, cysticercosis may involve the retina. Patients should be examined for retinal lesions before starting therapy for neurocysticercosis. 14. If retinal lesions are present, the need for anticysticercal therapy should be weighed against the risk of retinal damage caused by albendazole-induced changes to the lesions. 15. Some individuals, particularly young children, may have difficulty swallowing albendazole tablets whole. In such cases, the tablets should be crushed or chewed and taken with water. 16. Albendazole may cause harm to a fetus. Women of childbearing age should begin treatment only after a negative pregnancy test. 17. Women of childbearing age should be advised to avoid becoming pregnant while on albendazole or within one month of completing treatment. 18. Routine monitoring of blood counts and liver function tests should occur every two weeks during albendazole therapy due to the potential for liver or bone marrow harm. 19. Albendazole should be taken with food. 20. Albendazole has been associated with occasional, reversible reductions in total white blood cell counts in less than 1% of treated patients. 21. Rarely, more significant reductions in blood counts, such as granulocytopenia, agranulocytosis, or pancytopenia, may occur. 22. Blood counts should be performed at the start of each 28-day treatment cycle and every two weeks during therapy in all patients. 23. Patients with liver disease, including hepatic echinococcosis, are at increased risk of bone marrow suppression and require closer monitoring of blood counts. 24. Albendazole therapy should be discontinued in all patients if clinically significant decreases in blood cell counts occur. 25. Mild to moderate elevations in hepatic enzymes have been observed in approximately 16% of patients treated with albendazole during clinical trials. These elevations generally return to normal upon discontinuation of therapy. 26. There have been case reports of acute liver failure and hepatitis of uncertain causality associated with albendazole use. 27. Liver function tests (transaminases) should be performed before starting each treatment cycle and at least every two weeks during therapy. 28. If hepatic enzymes exceed twice the upper limit of normal, discontinuation of albendazole therapy should be considered based on individual patient circumstances. 29. Restarting albendazole treatment in patients whose hepatic enzymes have normalized off treatment is an individual decision that should consider the risk-benefit ratio of further albendazole use. 30. Laboratory tests should be performed frequently if albendazole treatment is restarted. 31. Patients with abnormal liver function test results are at increased risk for hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression. 32. Therapy should be discontinued if liver enzymes are significantly elevated or if clinically significant decreases in blood cell counts occur. 33. Albendazole does not inhibit theophylline metabolism in single doses but does induce cytochrome P450 1A in human hepatoma cells. Plasma concentrations of theophylline should be monitored during and after albendazole treatment. 34. Long-term carcinogenicity studies in mice and rats showed no evidence of increased tumor incidence in treated animals compared to controls. 35. Albendazole was negative in genotoxicity tests, including the Ames Salmonella/microsome plate mutation assay, Chinese hamster ovary chromosomal aberration test, and in vivo mouse micronucleus test. 36. In vitro BALB/3T3 cell transformation assays showed weak activity in the presence of metabolic activation but no activity in its absence. 37. Albendazole has been shown to be teratogenic in pregnant rats and rabbits, causing embryotoxicity and skeletal malformations at doses significantly higher than the recommended human dose. 38. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of albendazole use in pregnant women. Albendazole should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 39. Albendazole is excreted in animal milk, but it is unknown whether it is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administering albendazole to nursing women. 40. Experience in children under six years of age is limited. However, no significant problems have been encountered in treated infants and young children with hydatid disease or neurocysticercosis. 41. In five published studies involving pediatric patients as young as one year old, no significant problems were observed, and efficacy appeared similar to that in adults. 42. Experience in patients aged 65 years or older is limited. However, no specific problems associated with an older population have been observed in those treated for hydatid disease or neurocysticercosis.
